title: Sell Mineral Rights in Fayette County, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Fayette County, PA
metaDescription: Fayette County mineral owner? We buy Marcellus, Utica, and legacy gas interests around Uniontown, Connellsville, and the Route 40 corridor. Talk it through, no obligation.
heroLead: Fayette County land has been worked twice over — first for coal, then for gas — and the paperwork from both eras is usually still sitting in a drawer somewhere in Uniontown or Connellsville.
intro: My grandfather leased ground in Fayette County back when the Connellsville coke ovens were still glowing at night, and by the time gas rigs showed up decades later nobody in the family could find the original severance deed. That's Fayette County in a sentence: layers of history stacked on the same acre, and mineral owners trying to figure out which layer they actually own.

We buy mineral and royalty interests from owners across Fayette County — Uniontown, Fairchance, Farmington, Fayette City, Grindstone, Hopwood, Hiller, and the smaller crossroads in between. If you inherited a fractional interest from a coal-and-gas farm, or you're holding a Marcellus lease that stopped making sense once the deduction line items showed up, we'd like to hear about it.

sections.heading: Where Fayette County sits in the Marcellus play
paragraphs: Fayette is on the southern edge of the wet-gas Marcellus fairway that runs through Washington and Greene counties, so activity here has always been a bit more scattered than the core counties next door. Some ground has seen EQT and CNX laterals; other tracts, especially toward the eastern end of the county near the Laurel Highlands, have only ever produced from older, shallower formations like the Oriskany or Elk sands drilled decades before anyone said the word Marcellus.

That mix matters for value. A tract sitting under an active horizontal unit reads very differently than a legacy vertical well that's been stripper-producing since the 1970s. We look at both, because Fayette County owners often hold both kinds of interest in the same family, sometimes on the same parcel.

sections.heading: Coal-and-gas severance is the county's signature headache
paragraphs: Because Fayette County was mined so heavily for coal, a huge share of local mineral titles were severed generations ago in deeds that separated coal, oil, gas, and surface rights into different buckets — sometimes with different owners for each. Recorder of Deeds staff in Uniontown see this constantly: an owner comes in wanting to sell 'the minerals' and finds out coal went one direction in 1911 and oil and gas went another in 1940.

If your family's tract has this kind of history, sorting out exactly what interest you hold before you sell protects you from underselling — or from a deal falling apart at closing because the chain of title has a gap nobody caught.

sections.heading: Post-production deductions and the impact fee
paragraphs: Fayette County owners with active Marcellus leases have the same complaint I hear across southwestern PA: a royalty statement that starts at 1/8 or higher on paper, then gets whittled down by gathering, compression, and dehydration charges before the check ever hits the mailbox. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a 1/8 floor on the gross lease royalty, but it doesn't ban post-production deductions outright, and cases like Kilmer v. Elexco left plenty of room for operators to keep charging them depending on how the lease is worded.

Act 13 impact fees are a separate pot of money — paid by the driller per well, distributed to counties and municipalities for infrastructure and emergency services, not to individual mineral owners. It's worth knowing the difference before you go looking for that money in your royalty statement, because it was never going to show up there.

sections.heading: What we actually pay for
paragraphs: We buy producing royalty interests, non-producing minerals under lease, and in some cases unleased mineral acreage, whether it's your full interest or a fractional share inherited alongside cousins. Pricing depends on things that change tract to tract and month to month — well performance, decline curve, lease terms, remaining term on any Act 13-fee wells nearby, and current market activity — so we won't throw out a number before we've looked at your actual documents.

Bring what you have, even if it's incomplete. A lot of Fayette County families are working from a partial abstract, an old lease from a previous generation, or a single royalty check stub. We've pieced together stranger files than that.

faqs.question: I have a coal deed and a separate oil and gas deed for the same land in Fayette County — which one do you buy?
faqs.answer: We buy oil, gas, and mineral interests, not coal. If your family's severance split coal from oil and gas generations ago, we'd only be interested in the oil and gas side, and we can help you figure out which document actually controls that interest.

faqs.question: My well in Fayette County hasn't produced in years. Is my royalty interest worth anything?
faqs.answer: Possibly, especially if the lease is still held and the tract sits near active Marcellus development. A shut-in or marginal well doesn't automatically mean the underlying mineral interest has no value — it depends on nearby activity and remaining lease terms, so it's worth a conversation rather than assuming.

faqs.question: What is the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act and does it apply to my lease?
faqs.answer: It's a Pennsylvania law setting a 1/8 floor on gross royalty for oil and gas leases signed after it took effect. Older leases may not be covered the same way, and post-production deduction language still varies by lease, which is why we read the actual document rather than assuming a standard result.

faqs.question: Do I need to go through the Fayette County Recorder of Deeds before selling?
faqs.answer: We typically pull and review the recorded chain ourselves as part of due diligence, but if you already have deeds, probate records, or a prior title opinion, sharing those upfront speeds things along and helps us give you a more accurate number sooner.

faqs.question: I inherited a fractional interest with several cousins. Can you buy just my share?
faqs.answer: Yes. Fractional interests from inherited Fayette County farms are common, and we regularly buy one heir's share without requiring the whole family to sell together.
